passage: Rain kept the kindergarten indoors, so twenty children played musical statues in a room meant for ten. Pallavi, five, spun with her arms wide, then pulled them in when her elbow brushed Mridul. When the music stopped, she froze on one foot, wobbling, and put a hand on the wall instead of grabbing him. Mridul was hugging everyone who froze near him. A boy squirmed away. Pallavi said, "He doesn't want a hug. Ask first." Mridul let go and froze with his hands on his own knees.

qa.q: What game were the children playing?
qa.a: They were playing musical statues.

qa.q: Why might Pallavi have pulled her arms in after brushing Mridul?
qa.a: She noticed she had touched him and seemed to want to keep out of the other children's space in the crowded room.

qa.q: How could the teacher make the game safer in a crowded room?
qa.a: She could mark a spot for each child with tape or chalk and remind everyone to ask before touching.

qa.q: What was it like for the boy who squirmed away?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable being hugged, and Pallavi's words helped his wish to be noticed without him having to shout.

grounding: It shows a child keeping balance, protecting others' space and speaking up for a peer's body boundary during an active game.

passage: In the colony park in Hyderabad, Lakshmi and Uday were playing hopscotch on squares chalked by the watchman's son. Lakshmi hopped to seven on one foot, arms out like wings, then tipped and landed with both feet down. "Again!" she said. When Uday's turn came he started hopping right behind her. "Wait, I'm too near," Lakshmi said, stepping back so he wouldn't crash into her. Later a girl tugged Lakshmi's plait to tease her. "Don't pull my hair, it hurts," Lakshmi said. The girl let go and said sorry.

qa.q: Which square did Lakshmi reach before she tipped over?
qa.a: She hopped to square seven before she tipped.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi thinking when she said, "Wait, I'm too near"?
qa.a: She seemed to realise they might collide and wanted to give Uday room to hop safely.

qa.q: How could an adult support Lakshmi when someone pulls her hair?
qa.a: Praise her clear words and back her up calmly, while helping the other child practise asking before touching.

qa.q: How did the girl who pulled the plait learn something here?
qa.a: Hearing "it hurts" directly showed her the tease was not fun for Lakshmi, so she stopped and said sorry.

grounding: It shows a child balancing in a hopping game, keeping safe distance and stating her own body boundary.

passage:
"Tickle monster!" Tushar pounced, fingers wiggling.
Nikita shrieked, then went stiff. "Stop. Stop, Tushar."
He froze, hands in the air. "But you were laughing."
"Now I'm not."
Papa looked up from his tea. "What did she say?"
"Stop," Tushar mumbled, shuffling back. "Can I tickle your feet only?"
"No. But we can do the pillow jump."
"Okay! You go first. I'll stand back here so you don't land on me."
Nikita bounced off the sofa cushion, wobbled and caught her balance.
"Wow, you didn't fall!" Tushar cheered.

qa.q: What game did Nikita suggest instead of tickling?
qa.a: She suggested the pillow jump.

qa.q: Why did Tushar say "But you were laughing"?
qa.a: He was confused, because laughing looked like fun to him, and he may have felt a little stung at being stopped.

qa.q: What would you advise Tushar about tickling next time?
qa.a: Ask first, and stop the moment someone says stop, even if they were laughing a second ago.

qa.q: What is it like for Nikita when Tushar freezes at once?
qa.a: She learns her "stop" is respected, which likely makes her happy to keep playing with him.

grounding: It shows siblings honouring a spoken body boundary and giving each other space to balance in active play.

passage:
Coach's note, Saturday sports hour, Lokesh Sir
Pema did well on the balance beam today, arms out, eyes on the far end. In 'traffic lights' she stopped when a slower child was in front of her instead of pushing through. When the group was making a circle, she asked her neighbour, 'Can I hold your hand?' and waited for a nod. I pointed this out to the group. 👍

qa.q: What did Pema do when a slower child was in front of her?
qa.a: She stopped instead of pushing through.

qa.q: What does Pema waiting for a nod suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: It suggests she understood that her neighbour's hand and body belong to them, so she wanted permission first.

qa.q: How could Lokesh Sir help the other children learn from Pema?
qa.a: He could make asking before touching part of every circle game, praising children when they do it.

qa.q: How might the neighbour feel being asked before their hand is held?
qa.a: They would likely feel respected and comfortable, since they got a choice.

grounding: Illustrates a child keeping balance, managing personal space and respecting peers' bodily boundaries.

passage: After the rice harvest, the children raced along the narrow mud bunds between fields. Baljeet ran with arms out like wings, wobbling but never falling in. When Kunal tripped ahead of her, she slowed and leaned sideways so she wouldn't bump him. Later, playing train, Kunal said, 'Don't pull my shirt, it hurts.' Baljeet let go and held his shoulders lightly instead. 'Choo-choo,' she said.

qa.q: Where did the children race after the harvest?
qa.a: They raced along the narrow mud bunds between fields.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet let go of Kunal's shirt?
qa.a: She understood he did not like it and cared that she was hurting him, so she changed how she held on.

qa.q: What could an older cousin do to support this kind of play?
qa.a: They could praise Baljeet for listening and remind all children to check before grabbing each other in games.

qa.q: What would change if Baljeet had ignored Kunal's words?
qa.a: Kunal might feel hurt and not want to play, and the game could turn into a fight.

grounding: Shows a child balancing in active play and respecting a peer's body when asked, in a rural setting.

passage: In a Madrid schoolyard, Javier, five, was playing tag with Jin. Every time he tagged her, he grabbed her whole arm and nearly pulled them both over. "Too hard," Jin said. "Just touch." Javier stopped. Next time he reached out, tapped her shoulder with two fingers, and ran the other way, arms out for balance as he turned. Jin laughed and chased him. At the end of the game he stood an arm's length away to say bye.

qa.q: What did Jin tell Javier to do instead of grabbing?
qa.a: "Just touch."

qa.q: What might Javier have felt when Jin said "Too hard"?
qa.a: He may have felt a bit surprised or sorry, but he took it seriously and changed straight away.

qa.q: How could a teacher support what Javier learned?
qa.a: Praise him for listening and practise "gentle tag" with the whole group.

qa.q: How might Jin feel when Javier taps her with two fingers?
qa.a: Relieved and respected, and happy to keep playing with him.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to keep his tag gentle and respect a peer's body while staying balanced in the game.

passage: In the school's PE period, Madhuri, the teacher, gave each child a hula hoop. "Stand in your bubble. Move around without popping anyone else's." Deepika, five, walked, then skipped, carefully keeping her hoop from bumping others. When her friend dropped his hoop and she ran to hug him, he stepped back. "No hug." Deepika froze, then nodded. "Okay. High five?" He smiled and held up his hand.

qa.q: What did Madhuri give each child?
qa.a: A hula hoop.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she froze after "No hug"?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a little hurt, but she accepted his choice.

qa.q: Which choice by Deepika worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering a high five instead, because it kept the friendship warm while respecting his wish.

qa.q: How does Deepika's friend experience her response?
qa.a: He feels his "no" was respected, which makes him happy to connect in another way.

grounding: Shows a young child keeping to her own space in a movement game and respecting a friend's body boundary.

passage: I'm Ramesh, the watchman at the apartment gate. Every evening I see the children playing stuck-in-the-mud. Madhuri, five, is fast and good at dodging without bumping into anyone. Yesterday, when she freed a boy, he said, "Stop, you're pulling my shirt." She let go straight away and stepped back. She didn't argue. After that she just tapped his hand. I can't know what she thought, but the game went on without a fight.

qa.q: What game do the children play every evening?
qa.a: Stuck-in-the-mud.

qa.q: What might Madhuri have felt when the boy said "Stop"?
qa.a: Maybe a little embarrassed, but she seemed to care about his comfort, since she let go straight away without arguing.

qa.q: How could the children's parents build on this?
qa.a: Tell Madhuri they noticed she stopped when asked, and remind all the children that "stop" means stop.

qa.q: How does Ramesh see Madhuri's reaction?
qa.a: Ramesh sees she respected the boy's wish quickly, while admitting nobody can know her thoughts.

grounding: Shows a young child dodging with good balance and stopping when a peer says she is pulling, seen by a watchman.

passage:
Monday. At circle time, Nandini, five, keeps squeezing between friends and bumping elbows. Tina cries, "She's too close!"
Wednesday. Indu Ma'am teaches "bubble space": arms out, turn slowly, don't pop anyone's bubble. Nandini spins carefully, giggling, and shifts back.
Friday. During musical statues, Nandini runs, stops, wobbles, but keeps her balance and her space. When she wants to hug Tina, she asks first. Tina says no. Nandini nods and hugs her teddy instead.

qa.q: What does Indu Ma'am teach on Wednesday?
qa.a: Bubble space.

qa.q: What might Nandini have felt when Tina said no to the hug?
qa.a: Nandini was probably a little disappointed but accepted it calmly.

qa.q: How did 'bubble space' help Nandini?
qa.a: Stretching her arms and turning showed her how much room others need, so she stopped bumping.

qa.q: How might Tina feel when Nandini asks before hugging?
qa.a: Tina probably felt respected and safe, able to say no.

grounding: Over a week, a five-year-old learns personal space, balance in games and asking before hugging.

passage: The lane outside their Goa house was crowded and slippery on Holi afternoon, and Lalit, five, was covered in green. His friend Maria from the next house had come out in a new white frock. Lalit ran at her with a fistful of colour, slipped on the wet tiles, and caught himself on the gate. Maria stepped back. "No colour on me! Stop!" Lalit stopped, fist still raised. He looked at her frock. Then he rubbed the colour on his own cheeks instead. "Okay. Only me." Maria laughed.

qa.q: What was Maria wearing?
qa.a: A new white frock.

qa.q: What might Lalit have felt when Maria said stop?
qa.a: Lalit was probably disappointed for a moment, but chose to respect her.

qa.q: What did Lalit get right, and how can adults reinforce it?
qa.a: He stopped the moment Maria said no and put the colour on himself; adults can praise him for listening to 'stop'.

qa.q: How might Maria feel when Lalit stops?
qa.a: Maria probably felt relieved and respected, and laughed.

grounding: On a crowded Holi afternoon, a five-year-old keeps his balance and honours a friend's 'stop'.

passage: At the Christmas party in their Bengaluru apartment clubhouse, the children played musical chairs. Kiran, six, loved to win. When the music stopped, he dived for a chair and nearly knocked Uma off. "Ow! You pushed me!" Kiran froze. The uncle running the game paused the music. Kiran looked at Uma rubbing her arm. "Sorry. I'll wait for my own chair." Next round he ran, stopped, balanced on one foot, and sat only when there was an empty seat.

qa.q: What game did the children play?
qa.a: Musical chairs.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when he froze?
qa.a: Kiran felt startled and sorry after hurting Uma.

qa.q: How did Kiran change his play after pushing Uma?
qa.a: He apologised and then only sat on an empty chair, controlling his body and keeping his space.

qa.q: How might Uma feel after Kiran's apology?
qa.a: Uma probably felt better and more willing to keep playing.

grounding: At a Christmas party game, a six-year-old learns to control his body and respect a friend's space.

passage:
"Let's play statue!" Gurleen said. It was a cold Lohri afternoon, and they were in the courtyard.

"Freeze!" said Eshaan, and bumped into her.

"Too close, Eshaan. I need space for my arms."

Eshaan stepped back. "Like this?"

"Yes. Now freeze!"

They both froze, arms out, wobbling on one leg.

"You're falling!" Gurleen laughed.

"No, I'm balancing!"

qa.q: What game did Gurleen and Eshaan play?
qa.a: They played statue.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when Eshaan bumped into her?
qa.a: Gurleen was a bit annoyed and uncomfortable, needing more space for her arms.

qa.q: How could an adult support children in respecting each other's space?
qa.a: Remind them to leave space, and praise them when they step back after being asked.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel when Gurleen asked for space?
qa.a: Eshaan seemed fine with it and stepped back, happy to keep playing.

grounding: On a Lohri afternoon, two children play statue, keep their balance, and respect each other's personal space.

passage:
Sports practice note, spring.

In today's hopping race, Farida kept her balance on one foot all the way, even when the others wobbled. At the end, she stopped before bumping into Rani, who had fallen.

Later, she asked Rani, "Can I hug you?" Rani shook her head, and Farida just held out her hand instead.

I praised her for asking. — Deepak

qa.a: Farida just held out her hand instead.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt when Rani said no to a hug?
qa.a: Farida may have felt a little disappointed, but she respected Rani's choice.

qa.q: How did Deepak support Farida's respect for boundaries?
qa.a: He praised her for asking before hugging.

qa.q: How might Rani feel when Farida asked before hugging?
qa.a: Rani would likely feel respected and safe that her choice was honoured.

grounding: A sports note records a child keeping her balance, avoiding a collision, and respecting a peer's choice about touch.

passage:
After the harvest, the children in the village near Nashik played kho-kho on the empty threshing ground. Abhinav was the chaser.

He ran fast, but slowed as he reached Alka and tapped her shoulder gently instead of pushing.

"Out!" he said.

Alka laughed and sat down. "You didn't push me this time."

"Last time you fell," Abhinav said. "So I tap now."

qa.q: Where did the children play kho-kho?
qa.a: They played on the empty threshing ground.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav slow down before tagging Alka?
qa.a: Abhinav felt concerned and a little guilty because Alka fell last time, so he wanted to keep her safe.

qa.q: How could adults support Abhinav's careful play?
qa.a: Praise him for tapping gently and remind all players to keep control of their bodies.

qa.q: How might Alka see Abhinav's change?
qa.a: Alka noticed and appreciated that he didn't push her this time.

grounding: After the harvest, a child in a village game controls his speed and taps gently, honouring a peer's body.

passage: On Three Kings' Day, the park in Madrid was full of children with new toys. Clara and Pablo played tag round the frozen fountain. Pablo ran fast, but at each corner he slowed and leaned in so he wouldn't slip on the ice. When he caught Clara, he grabbed her in a tight hug. "Stop, too squeezy!" she said. Pablo let go at once and stepped back. "Sorry. Tag with one finger?" Clara grinned. "One finger. Go!" This time he tapped her shoulder lightly and ran.

qa.q: What did Clara say when Pablo hugged her?
qa.a: "Stop, too squeezy!"

qa.q: Why did Pablo let go at once and step back?
qa.a: He wanted Clara to feel comfortable and seemed a little embarrassed that his hug had been too tight.

qa.q: What could an adult say to encourage how Pablo handled it?
qa.a: They could say, "You listened when Clara said stop, and you found a new way to play."

qa.q: How does Clara feel when Pablo suggests "one finger"?
qa.a: Clara feels respected and happy to keep playing, since her "stop" was heard straight away. 😊

grounding: Shows a young child keeping his balance on ice during a winter game and respecting a friend's body boundary.
